title: Tzav: the fire shall not go out (Leviticus 6:6)
hookLine: "it shall not go out"; a fire tended every day

lines: A FIRE THAT NEVER GOES OUT.
cards: Anyone who has kept a fire going knows it's never a one-time job. A campfire, a wood stove in winter, a fireplace on a long night: you don't light it and walk away.
You feed it, add another log, keep the coals alive till morning, and if you forget for too long, it's gone, and you start over with cold hands.
This week's portion, Tzav, gives the priests a fire like that: a fire on the altar that is never allowed to go out.

teach.b: Tzav means command, and Rashi notes it's a word of urgency: do this, and keep doing it, now and for generations. Then comes the fire: "Fire shall be kept burning upon the altar continually; it shall not go out."
The Hebrew for continually is tamid, always. So every morning the priest laid fresh wood on the altar, whether or not there was anything special to offer. Ordinary days, rainy days, days nobody came.
The fire was the constant. Then a detail from the Talmud. Tradition says fire came down from heaven onto the altar at its dedication.
You'd think that settles it: God's own fire, burning by itself.
But the rabbis say that even so, it was still a commandment to bring ordinary, human fire every day. Heaven provides the spark. People still bring the wood.
Some later teachers read this as a picture of the inner life.
The altar is the heart, they said, and a fire there needs tending every day, or it fades. Not because it was never lit, but because nobody fed it.

So the first week of Leviticus closes: where children began, the small alef, korban as nearness, the poor person's flour, the salt of the covenant, a leader's mistakes, and now a fire that never goes out.

how: Synagogues commonly hang a ner tamid, an ever-burning light, above the ark, and the idea of tamid, a daily, unbroken practice, is often applied to prayer and study.

o: wood: the fuel laid on each morning
fire: the flame kept burning on the altar
command: a word of urgency, for always

games.q: what's inside the fire — tap the pairs.

s: the altar fire was lit only on holy days
it burned continually, tamid, and was tended every morning.
the rabbis say ordinary fire was still brought, even though fire came from heaven
heaven provides the spark; people still bring the wood.
tzav is an ordinary word with no special urgency

games.q: you're a priest. tradition says the altar fire came down from heaven. it's morning, and the fire is burning. what do you do?
o: leave it: heaven's fire takes care of itself.
add wood, as you do every morning.
let it burn down and relight it on festivals.
games.why: the priest lays wood on the altar every morning. the rabbis say: even though fire came from heaven, bringing human fire is still a commandment.

practice: Choose one thing in your life that only stays alive if you feed it a little every day: a friendship, a skill, a prayer, a garden, a language, a marriage.
Picture the smallest daily log you could add, a text, ten minutes, one page, one kind word, something you could manage even on a bad day. Hold that one log in your hands for a while.

wordCard.voice: Tzav. Command, with urgency. The portion where the altar's fire is tended every day, and never allowed to go out.

carryVoice: Your line: keep the fire. Small logs count, one day after another. Day three hundred eighty-five, done.
